newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mafia runs 40 pct of Russian economy - US study.
newsitem.headline: Mafia runs 40 pct of Russian economy - US study.

text.p: A U.S. report has concluded that more than 40 percent of the Russian economy is controlled by Mafia-style groups, with organised crime fuelling capital flight of at least $50 billion since 1991.
The report said the criminal groups had taken advantage of Russia's huge privatisation programme and that their activites were having a devastating effect on the economy.

Although President Boris Yeltsin has pursued a tough anti-corruption campaign, the report by Louise Shelley, a law professor at American University, Washington D.C., said organised crime had seized control of more than 40 percent of the total Russian economy.
Mafia-style groups had taken an even greater share in sectors such as consumer markets, real estate and banking, by taking advantage of the privatisation programme.
Russia has transferred about 70 percent of enterprises to private hands since 1992.

"Russian organised crime groups secured a massive transfer of state property because the privatisation occurred rapidly, on a huge scale, without legal safeguards, and without transparency," said the study, published in the latest issue of the World Bank newsletter Transition.
"These groups used force, if necessary, but relied mainly on their large financial assets and their close ties to the former Communist Party elite, the military and the banking sector."
As a result organised crime now dominates the legitimate and illegitimate economies simultaneously, it said.

"Organised crime... discourages foreign investment, deprives the country of its tax base, dominates the banking sector and financial markets, and exacerbates the already widespread problem of corruption," the study said.
"But probably the most damaging aspect of Russian organised crime activity is its contribution to large-scale capital flight," it said.
Colombian drug traffickers repatriate most of their profits and the Italian mafia invested much of its profits domestically.
But Russian organised crime groups prefer to deposit most of their proceeds in foreign countries, establishing off-shore havens, it said.
Conservative estimates of capital flight since 1991 are more than $50 billion, and one specialist at a recent Interior Ministry conference reported a figure of $150 billion, it said.
"A minimum of 40 percent of the estimated $2 billion in monthly capital flight is attributable to organised crime groups," it said.
Suggesting ways of countering the problem, the study said efforts to decriminalise the economy should define the problem more broadly than money laundering.

Donor nations and institutions must coordinate their help in setting up regulation and enforcement mechanisms for effective governing of financial institutions and markets. Aid programmes must identify areas which have managed to avoid massive criminalisation.
"Building integrity in the banking sector and in financial markets must be a key objective of any assistance programme to combat Russian organised crime," it said.
The capital flight problem dwarfs the lack of foreign investment, which totals only $6 billion since 1991, the study said.
Organised crime also damages Russia's tax base. Apart from not paying taxes, organised crime groups usurp the state's tax collection role, depriving it of needed resources.

Recent research shows that duties are paid on only 35 of every 1,000 cars imported into Russia. Regional crime bosses control customs warehouses in many part of Russia and have customs officials on their payrolls.
Organised crime has also infiltrated the Russian banking system, and banks who refuse to launder money cannot competewith banks that do, it said
